question: An occlusion forms when:

options.text: The faster cold front catches the warm front, lifting the warm air off the surface
Two anticyclones meet and squeeze the depression between them
The faster warm front overtakes the cold front, trapping the cold air beneath
A front becomes stationary over mountains and the two air masses mix

explanation: Because the cold front moves faster than the warm front, the warm sector narrows until the two fronts merge and the warm air is lifted aloft.

question: The point where the occluded front meets the warm and cold fronts is called the:

options.text: Warm sector apex, or wave crest
Col, or neutral point of the system
Frontal wave crest, or kink
Point of occlusion, or triple point

explanation: The triple point moves away from the depression centre along the warm sector as the occlusion process continues.

question: Once a depression has occluded, the warm sector air:

options.text: Sinks beneath the cold air on both sides
Is lifted off the ground and lies above the occlusion
Disappears completely, mixing into the cold air
Remains at the surface between the two fronts as before

explanation: At the surface, the occluded front separates two cold air masses; the warm air remains above as a trough of warm air aloft.

question: Whether an occlusion is warm or cold is decided by:

options.text: The speed of the cold front compared with that of the warm front
Whether the precipitation at the occlusion falls as rain or snow
Whether the air ahead of the warm front or behind the cold front is colder
The season of the year alone: warm in summer and cold in winter

explanation: Whichever of the two cold air masses is colder will stay at the surface and undercut the other.

question: A warm occlusion forms when:

options.text: The air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front
The warm sector air is colder than both
The air ahead of the warm front is colder than the air behind the cold front
The two cold air masses have exactly the same temperature

explanation: The less cold air behind the cold front rides up over the colder air ahead of the warm front.

question: Over western Europe, warm occlusions are most common in:

options.text: All seasons equally, as the type does not depend on season
Winter, when very cold continental air lies ahead of the warm front
Summer, when the continent ahead of the warm front is very warm
Spring only, when the sea is at its coldest

explanation: In winter the continental air ahead of the depression is often colder than the maritime air behind the cold front.

question: On a chart, the line of a warm occlusion:

options.text: Is drawn as a separate line with no relationship to either front
Is shown only by a trough
Continues along the line of the cold front, with the warm front discontinuous above it
Continues along the line of the warm front, with the cold front discontinuous above it

explanation: In a warm occlusion the cold front rides up over the warm front, so the surface front continues the warm front's line.

question: In a warm occlusion, most of the precipitation falls:

options.text: Ahead of the surface position of the occlusion
Nowhere, as warm occlusions are dry
Behind the surface position of the occlusion
Only directly over the triple point

explanation: The structure resembles a warm front, with a shallow upper cold front ahead of the surface position, so the rain belt lies largely ahead.

question: A cold occlusion forms when:

options.text: The warm sector is colder than both cold air masses
The occlusion moves over the sea
The air ahead of the warm front is colder than the air behind the cold front
The air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front

explanation: The colder air behind the cold front undercuts the less cold air ahead of the warm front, so the surface front follows the cold front.

question: Over western Europe, cold occlusions are most common in:

options.text: Winter, when the continental air ahead is very cold and dry under a high
Never over Europe, only over North America
Summer, when the continental air ahead is warmer than the air behind
Only in spring, when the land is warming

explanation: In summer the continent heats up, so the air ahead of the warm front is less cold than the Atlantic air behind the cold front.

question: In a cold occlusion, most of the precipitation falls:

options.text: Only at the triple point
Behind the surface position of the occlusion
Only far ahead of the warm front
Ahead of the surface position of the occlusion

explanation: The structure resembles a cold front, so most of the weather is concentrated near and behind the surface front.

question: On a chart, the line of a cold occlusion:

options.text: Follows the line of the cold front, with the warm front discontinuous
Is not shown on surface charts at all
Is always drawn using the stationary front symbol
Follows the line of the warm front, with the cold front discontinuous

explanation: In a cold occlusion the cold front stays at the surface, so the occluded front follows on from it.

question: A station reports 3°C ahead of an occlusion and 6°C behind it. This is most likely:

options.text: A stationary front
A warm occlusion
A cold occlusion
A warm front only

explanation: The air ahead is colder than the air behind, so the air behind will ride over it: a warm occlusion.

question: A station reports 12°C ahead of an occlusion and 8°C behind it. This is most likely:

options.text: A col
A warm occlusion
A cold occlusion
A warm front

explanation: The colder air behind undercuts the warmer air ahead, so this is a cold occlusion.

question: Weather at an active occlusion is often severe because:

options.text: The weather is concentrated in a narrower band, often with embedded CB
Occlusions only occur in summer, when convection is strongest
There is never any precipitation to wash out the cloud
The air in an occlusion is always very dry and unstable at all levels

explanation: Cumuliform cloud from the cold front is pushed into the stratiform cloud of the warm front, giving embedded cumulonimbus that may be hidden from view.

question: The main flying hazard associated with an active occlusion is:

options.text: Clear air turbulence near the jet stream, with no cloud
Dust haze carried up from the surface by the occlusion's winds
Radiation fog forming at the occlusion overnight only
Embedded cumulonimbus within layer cloud, with icing and turbulence

explanation: Embedded storms cannot be seen visually; weather radar is needed. Icing can be severe through a deep layer.

question: Because an occlusion forms late in a depression's life, when movement is slowing, its weather:

options.text: Moves faster than the original fronts
May persist over an area for a long time
Is always very light
Passes quickly within an hour

explanation: Slow movement means prolonged cloud and precipitation at any one place.

question: A warm occlusion over Europe in winter can carry a particular risk of:

options.text: Haar along the east coasts
Dust storms carried westwards from the steppes of Russia
Rain ice, from rain falling into very cold air below
Tropical revolving storms

explanation: Rain from the upper warm air falls into the cold continental air below, where it may become supercooled and freeze on impact.

question: As a depression decays, its occlusion often becomes:

options.text: A warm front again
A tropical revolving storm
More active, with severe thunderstorms along its length
Inactive, giving little more than some cloud

explanation: Once the temperature contrast is lost and ascent weakens, the occlusion fades away (frontolysis).

question: A back-bent occlusion is:

options.text: Part of the occlusion curling back round the centre, giving rain in the cold air
A trough lying some distance ahead of the surface warm front
An occlusion that has become stationary over a range of mountains
A cold front that has reversed and is moving backwards towards the warm air

explanation: As the triple point moves away, the occlusion can wrap back round the centre for 100–200 nm, bringing unexpected rain behind the cold front.

question: The characteristics of an occlusion:

options.text: Always identical to those of a cold front, whatever the type
Free of precipitation, because the warm air is no longer at the surface
Always identical to those of a warm front, whatever the type
Variable: like a warm or cold front according to type, and often ill defined

explanation: An occlusion's weather depends on its type and stage of development, so forecasting it is difficult.

question: In the Northern Hemisphere, an occluding depression tends to:

options.text: Move due east at a constant speed
Slow down and curve to the left (anticlockwise)
Move steadily towards the Equator
Speed up and curve to the right (clockwise)

explanation: Occluded depressions slow and often curve northwards, moving round their own circulation, before filling.

question: The future position of the point of occlusion can be estimated by:

options.text: Assuming it stays in the same place for the whole forecast period
Moving it towards the highest pressure on the chart
Moving both fronts forward at their expected speeds to see where they meet
Moving it at the speed and direction of the surface wind at the centre

explanation: Because the cold front catches up with the warm front, the meeting point moves outwards along the warm sector.

question: A typical polar front depression takes about how long to reach its lowest pressure?

options.text: About 4 days
About 4 weeks
About 4 hours
About 12 hours

explanation: Development to maturity takes a few days; filling and decay often take a week or more after that.

question: Depressions affecting the British Isles typically:

options.text: Form and decay within a single day over the Irish Sea
Form over Scandinavia, move west across the Atlantic and fill over eastern Canada
Form off the US coast or mid-Atlantic, deepen over the Atlantic and fill over Scandinavia
Form over the Sahara, move north across Spain and fill over Iceland

explanation: The westerlies carry them across the Atlantic. They are usually occluded and filling by the time they reach northern Europe.

question: New depressions in a family most often form:

options.text: As secondaries at the triple point or on a trailing cold front
In the eye of a tropical cyclone as it moves north
Over the poles, where the coldest air is found
At the centre of the subtropical high, as it slowly weakens

explanation: A trailing cold front crossing a coastline or mountains, or the triple point of an occluded depression, are favourite places for new waves to develop.

question: Filling and decay of a depression can take:

options.text: Several months, drifting slowly towards the pole
10 days or more, until absorbed by another system
Exactly 24 hours, following the daily heating cycle
Less than an hour, once the occlusion is complete

explanation: Depressions take much longer to die away than to develop, gradually losing their fronts and filling.

question: An aircraft flies through a warm occlusion in winter at FL080 from the cold air ahead of it. It is likely to meet:

options.text: Only thin cirrus, because the occlusion is a high-level feature
Clear skies throughout, because the warm air has been lifted far away from the surface
A sudden improvement in visibility on entering the frontal cloud
Thickening layer cloud, continuous precipitation, maybe embedded CB, and icing

explanation: A warm occlusion behaves much like a warm front, with an added upper cold front that may contain embedded convection.

question: The warm air of an occluded depression, lifted off the surface, is sometimes shown on charts as:

options.text: A sea breeze front along the coast
A trough of warm air aloft (trowal)
A ridge of cold air at the surface
A col between the two cold air masses

explanation: The warm air forms a tongue aloft above the occluded front, sometimes described as a trough of warm air aloft.

question: A depression has occluded completely and the triple point has moved far from the centre. At the centre, the surface air:

options.text: Has no temperature contrast aloft or at the surface
Is entirely warm sector air
Is entirely cold air, with the warm air lifted aloft
Is tropical continental air

explanation: Once occluded, the depression's centre lies in cold air; this is why old depressions are cold-cored and slow moving.

question: Embedded cumulonimbus is a particular hazard of occlusions because:

options.text: The cold front's convective cloud is pushed into the warm front's layer cloud
Cumulonimbus at occlusions is always visible from a great distance
Occlusions only form in clear air, so the storms within them are invisible
Occlusions have no layer cloud for the storms to hide in

explanation: Merging cloud systems mean storm cells can be hidden in extensive stratiform cloud, so they cannot be avoided visually.

question: When an occluding depression is held back by a mountain range such as southern Greenland or Norway, a common result is:

options.text: Immediate filling of all nearby depressions
The formation of a tropical revolving storm
The occlusion turning back into a warm front
A new secondary low at the triple point

explanation: The blocked fronts encourage a new centre to develop at the tip of the warm sector.

question: The symbol for an occluded front on a surface chart shows:

options.text: Semicircles only, on the side towards which it moves
Triangles only, on the side towards which it moves
Triangles and semicircles on the same side of the line
Triangles and semicircles on opposite sides of the line

explanation: The combined symbol points in the direction of movement. Symbols on opposite sides indicate a stationary front.

question: Which part of a polar front depression gives the most persistent weather late in its life?

options.text: The high pressure ridge behind it
The fast-moving cold front far from the centre
The warm sector far to the south
The slow-moving occlusion near the centre

explanation: Occlusions form as depressions slow down, so their cloud and rain can stay over an area for a long time.

question: An occlusion is described as "warm" or "cold" according to:

options.text: Which cold air mass, ahead or behind, is colder
The season in which it occurs
The temperature of the warm sector air above it
Whether it produces rain or snow

explanation: The colder of the two air masses stays at the surface and determines the type.
